passages.title: Leo at the Skate Park
sentences: On Saturday morning, Leo went to the skate park.
He took his new skateboard.
The park was quiet.
Leo rode up the big ramp.
He did his best trick.
Leo smiled and did the trick again.
At noon, he rode home for lunch.

passages.title: Sam and Pixel at the Harbor
sentences: After school on Monday, Sam took Pixel for a walk.
They went down to the harbor.
Pixel saw the boats.
Pixel barked at a big white ferry.
The ferry blew its horn.
Sam laughed.
Then they walked home for dinner.

credit.title: Sam and Pixel at the Harbor
credit.author: Learning to Fly (AI-drafted)

passages.title: Game Night
sentences: On Friday night, Ana and Ben played a new video game.
They sat on the big couch in their living room.
Ana drove a red race car.
Ben drove a blue race car.
Ana won the first race.
Ben won the next two races.
He jumped up and cheered.

passages.title: Priya Tests Her Rover
sentences: On Wednesday after school, Priya went to robotics club.
The club meets in Ms. Ortiz's science room at Harbor Middle School.
Priya was building a small rover with six wheels.
Today she wanted to test it on the floor.
She pressed the green button on the remote.
The rover rolled across the room and stopped by the door.
Ms. Ortiz clapped, and Priya grinned.
At 4:45 PM, Priya put the rover in her backpack and went home.

passages.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
sentences: One hot summer, an ant and a grasshopper lived in a big green field.
Every day, the ant carried seeds to her nest.
The grasshopper sat in the sun and sang songs.
"Come and sing with me," said the grasshopper.
"I am saving food for the winter," said the ant.
Then the cold winter came, and snow covered the field.
The ant had plenty of food in her nest.
The grasshopper was hungry, so he asked the ant for help.
The ant gave him some seeds.
The next summer, the grasshopper saved food too.

credit.title: The Ant and the Grasshopper
credit.author: Aesop, retold for Learning to Fly
credit.source: The Aesop for Children (1919), Library of Congress

passages.title: Match Day
sentences: Ana and Ben Diaz ate a quick lunch at home on Saturday.
After lunch, they packed their soccer bags.
Ana put in her shin guards and a water bottle.
Ben's left soccer shoe was missing, so the twins searched the whole house.
Finally, Ana found it underneath the couch.
Their dad drove them across Harbor Town.
Dad parked next to a wide green field with white lines and two big nets.
Their coach waved to them from a bench beside the field.
The game started at two o'clock, and the twins ran onto the grass.
Ben kicked the ball hard and scored the first goal of the match.

passages.title: Stars at Lantern Peaks
sentences: Sam had a big plan for Friday.
He wanted to see the planet Saturn through a real telescope.
After dinner, Sam and Grandma Rose rode the bus up into Lantern Peaks.
The sky turned dark blue, and Sam saw the first stars.
The bus stopped at the top of the hill, next to a white building with a round roof.
Inside, a scientist named Dr. Lee was pointing a giant telescope at the sky.
"Our observatory is the best place on the island to look at planets," she said.
Sam looked through the telescope and saw a tiny yellow ball with a ring around it.
He grinned and asked Grandma Rose to come and look.
They stayed until nine o'clock, and then they rode the last bus home.

passages.title: The Comic Contest
sentences: The comic contest at the Harbor Town library ended on Friday.
On Wednesday, Maya still had two pages left to draw.
After dinner that night, she sat at her desk and drew until her hand was tired.
On Thursday, she spent her lunch break in the school art room.
Ms. Ortiz walked past the door and stopped to look at the last page.
"Your rock monster is great," she said.
Maya smiled and colored the last box green.
Her comic was finally finished.
The next morning, on the last day of the contest, Maya carried it into the library.
She gave it to the librarian at the front desk, who put it on a table with forty other comics.

passages.title: After the Storm
sentences: A strong storm blew across Harbor Town on Sunday night.
Rain hit Sam's window for hours, and the wind bent the tall trees in the yard.
By the time the sun came up, the sky was clear and calm again.
Harbor Middle School was closed the next day, because the storm had left the building without electricity.
After breakfast, Grandma Rose said that Sam could take Pixel for a long walk if he stayed on the marked trails.
At nine o'clock, Sam clipped a leash to Pixel's collar, and they started up the trail into Story Woods.
He wanted to see how high the creek had risen near the old mill.
Halfway up the trail, a fallen tree was lying across the path.
Sam unfolded his map and found a second trail that curved around the back of the hill.
Pixel sniffed every log and puddle along the way.
Two hours after they left home, they finally reached the mill.
The creek beside it was wide and brown, and the old wooden wheel was turning faster than Sam had ever seen.
He took a photo of the wheel to show Grandma Rose at lunch.

passages.title: Priya's Test Day
sentences: The school science fair was only two days away, and Priya's rover still needed one more test.
On Saturday morning, she packed it carefully in a soft bag and rode her bike to Harbor Middle School.
The gym was locked on weekends, so she used the empty parking lot behind the building.
For an hour, she drove the rover around a path of orange cones.
It turned well, but the left front wheel squeaked on every corner.
Priya wrote the problem in her notebook and rode across town to Okafor's Bike Shop.
Mr. Okafor keeps a special oil for small moving parts, and he was happy to help.
He put two drops of oil on the wheel and spun it slowly with one finger.
The squeak was gone.
Priya thanked him, then walked next door to the Lighthouse Café, where she ate a cheese sandwich and drew a plan for a new robot arm.

passages.title: The Meteor Shower
sentences: Every year in late October, Earth passes through a long trail of dust left behind by a famous comet.
When tiny pieces of that dust hit the air high above the ground, they burn up and make bright streaks across the night sky.
Scientists call this event a meteor shower, and each streak is called a meteor.
This year, Ms. Ortiz decided that her science club would watch the shower from the hills behind Harbor Town.
The club met at the school gate on Friday, just as the sun was going down.
Sam brought a star map, Maya brought a sketchbook, and Leo brought three bags of popcorn.
A small yellow bus carried them up the winding road into Lantern Peaks.
Forty minutes later, it stopped beside the lookout, a flat, rocky place with a wooden fence and a wide view of the sky.
At first, the sky was too bright, because the moon was still shining above the hills.
Ms. Ortiz explained that the best time to look would come after the moon went down.
The students spread blankets on the cold ground and waited.
Sam used the time to find the stars of Orion on his map, because the meteors seem to fly out from that part of the sky.
Just before ten o'clock, the moon disappeared behind the hills, and the sky turned black.
Maya saw the first meteor, a thin silver line that lasted less than a second.
During the next hour, the club counted twenty-three more.
By the time the bus carried them back down to the school, it was almost midnight, and Leo had eaten every piece of popcorn.

passages.title: The Bake Sale
sentences: On Thursday morning, Harbor Middle School had a bake sale in the front hall.
Maya and Priya ran the cookie table before the first bell.
Grandma Rose had baked two trays of oat cookies for them.
Each cookie cost one dollar.
Students lined up with coins in their hands.
By the first bell, only three cookies were left.
At lunch, the girls sold the last three cookies to Ms. Ortiz.
After school, they took the money box to the school office.

passages.title: The Old Copper Mine
sentences: Ms. Ortiz's class had a science test on Monday.
The next morning, the whole class rode a bus to the far side of Lantern Peaks.
The bus stopped beside a gray stone building with a tall wooden tower.
A sign over the door said RIDGEWAY MINE MUSEUM.
A guide named Mr. Varga gave each student a hard hat with a lamp on the front.
Long ago, miners dug tunnels deep under this hill to find copper.
Copper is a metal that is used to make electric wires.
The miners broke off rock with copper in it and loaded it into carts on metal rails.
Mr. Varga led the class into the first tunnel, and Maya switched on her lamp.
The walls were cold and wet, and thin green lines ran through the gray rock.
Mr. Varga said that the green color came from copper.
Maya drew the green lines in her sketchbook.
At noon, the class ate lunch at picnic tables outside the museum.

passages.title: Tide Pool Morning
sentences: Twice a day, the sea pulls back from the rocky beach at the end of the harbor.
When the water goes out, small pools of seawater are left between the rocks.
These are called tide pools, and many sea animals live in them.
On Sunday, Sam and Maya sat on the seawall and waited for the tide to go out.
By ten o'clock, the rocks were dry enough to walk on.
Maya found a purple sea star holding on to the side of a deep pool.
Sam saw a hermit crab carrying an empty snail shell on its back.
A hermit crab uses an old shell as its home, and it moves into a bigger one as it grows.
Sam and Maya looked carefully, but they did not lift any animals out of the water.
When the tide came back in, they climbed up to the seawall and ate their lunch.

words.means: the rise and fall of the sea each day
a high stone edge built to hold back the waves

passages.title: The First Concert
sentences: On Wednesday afternoon, the music room at Harbor Middle School was full of noise.
Twenty students in the Grade 7 band were tuning their instruments at the same time, and every one of them sounded a little different.
Their teacher, a tall woman with a silver trumpet, tapped her music stand until the room went quiet.
Her name was Ms. Gray, and she had taught music at Harbor Middle School for ten years.
She reminded the students that their first concert of the year, with the Grade 6 band, would begin at seven o'clock the next evening, in the school gym.
By seven o'clock the next evening, every folding chair in the gym was full.
The band's drummer sat at the back, behind three drums and a shiny cymbal.
It was Leo Park, and he had never played in front of a crowd before.
Ms. Gray raised both hands, and the first song began.
Leo kept a steady beat, and the trumpets and flutes followed him.
When the last song ended, the families clapped for a long time.
The morning after the concert, Leo rode his skateboard to the skate park before school.
Sam was there with Pixel, and he told Leo that he had heard every drum beat from the last row.
Leo laughed and said that next time he would play even louder.

passages.title: The Dinosaur Hall
sentences: The new dinosaur hall at the Harbor Town museum opened on the first Saturday in September.
Sam and Maya took the early bus so that they could be at the door when it opened at nine o'clock.
In the middle of the hall stood the skeleton of a Triceratops, a plant-eating dinosaur with three horns on its face.
Its skull alone was longer than Sam is tall.
A sign said that Triceratops lived about sixty-six million years ago, near the end of the age of dinosaurs.
Behind a glass wall at the back of the hall, a woman in a white coat was cleaning a fossil with a tiny brush.
A sign on the glass said that she was a paleontologist, a scientist who studies fossils.
When she saw Sam and Maya watching, she came out to say hello.
Her name was Dr. Bell, and she let Maya hold a real fossil tooth.
She told them that most of the bones in the big skeleton were copies.
Real fossils are very heavy, and they can break easily.
Two hours after the doors opened, the hall was crowded.
Sam and Maya walked across the street to the Lighthouse Café.
While they waited for their sandwiches, Maya drew the Triceratops skull on a paper napkin.

passages.title: The Weather Station
sentences: Weather scientists watch the air pressure closely, because it often changes before the weather does.
Air pressure is the weight of the air pressing down on the land, and it is measured with a tool called a barometer.
When the pressure drops quickly, a storm is often on its way.
On the last Saturday in March, Sam and Priya climbed the steep path to the weather station on Lantern Peaks, beside the observatory.
They arrived at ten o'clock.
The station's only worker, a woman with a gray braid and a clipboard, was waiting at the door.
She was Dr. Lee, the scientist who also runs the big telescope next door, and she had asked the robotics club for two helpers.
First she showed them the anemometer, a set of small cups on a tall pole that spin faster when the wind blows harder.
Then she pointed at the barometer on the wall and explained that its needle had been moving down since early that morning.
Two hours after they arrived, the needle had dropped even further, and dark clouds were moving toward the island from the sea.
Dr. Lee decided that the children should go home before the rain began.
She drove them down the winding road in her small white truck and left them at the bus station in Harbor Town.
Sam walked the last few blocks to Rose's Bakery, where Grandma Rose was closing the shop for the day.
By the time he sat down at the window table with a cup of cocoa, heavy rain was falling on the street outside.
He watched the storm for an hour and thought about the needle on the barometer, which had warned them hours before the first drop fell.

passages.title: The Final on Gull Island
sentences: Ana and Ben had waited all spring for the final of the island soccer league.
Their team, the Harbor Hawks, would play the Gull Island Gulls on the last Sunday in May.
The final would be played on the Gulls' home field, so the whole team had to cross the bay by ferry.
The ferry left Harbor Town at nine o'clock in the morning and reached Gull Island 40 minutes later.
The field was a short walk from the dock, on a flat, grassy hill above the beach, where a crowd of families was already gathering.
The referee, a man in a black shirt with a whistle around his neck, was already checking the nets.
When he turned around, the twins saw that he was Mr. Okafor from the bike shop.
He explained that he had been a soccer referee for twenty years, since long before he opened his shop.
The game began one hour and twenty minutes after the ferry arrived.
Both teams defended carefully, and neither team scored during the first half.
Early in the second half, Ana passed the ball across the field, and Ben kicked it into the corner of the net.
That single goal was enough, and the Hawks won the championship by one goal to nothing.
On the ferry home that afternoon, the players shared orange slices and took turns holding the small silver cup.
Mr. Okafor sat at the back of the ferry and read a book, because he lives in Harbor Town too.

passages.title: A Snowman by the Slide
sentences: On Tuesday morning, deep snow covered Harbor Town.
There was no school that day.
Ana and Ben hurried to the park.
They made a big snowman by the slide.
Ben gave it a red hat.
Ana gave it two sticks for arms.
At noon, they walked home for hot tomato soup.

passages.title: Maya Plays Her Flute
sentences: After dinner on Wednesday, Maya went to her room.
She took her flute out of its case.
She played a slow song.
Then she played a fast song.
Her mom clapped from the kitchen.
Maya smiled and played the fast song again.
At eight o'clock, she put the flute away.

passages.title: The Coast Train
sentences: On Sunday morning, Sam and his dad walked to the train station in Harbor Town.
They got on the coast train at nine o'clock.
Sam sat by the window with his map on his lap.
The train ran beside the sea for a long time.
Sam saw fishing boats, black rocks and a tall lighthouse.
He marked each station on his map with a pencil.
At ten o'clock, the train stopped at Shell Beach.
Sam and his dad got off and walked on the sand.
They found three shells and a piece of green sea glass.
After lunch, they rode the train back home.

passages.title: Ducks at the Creek
sentences: On Saturday afternoon, Maya walked to the creek in Story Woods.
She brought her sketchbook and two pencils.
A mother duck was swimming near the bank.
Six brown ducklings swam in a line behind her.
Maya sat on a big flat rock and drew them.
Then a man with a gray dog came down the trail.
The ducks swam under some low branches.
Maya waited quietly until they came back out.
At four o'clock, she walked home and showed the drawing to her dad.

passages.title: The Chess Club
sentences: Every Monday after school, the chess club meets at the library.
This week, Ben and Leo sat at the table by the big window.
Ben played with the white pieces.
Leo played with the black pieces.
The game was slow, and both boys thought hard.
The librarian, Mrs. Hall, stopped to watch for a few minutes.
After forty minutes, Leo moved his queen and said, "Checkmate."
Ben shook his hand.
Then they set up the board and played again.

passages.title: Pizza on the Porch
sentences: On Friday evening, Priya and her dad made pizza in their kitchen.
Dad rolled out the dough on the counter.
Priya spread red sauce on top.
She added cheese, peppers and mushrooms.
Dad slid the pizza into the hot oven.
Twenty minutes later, the cheese was brown and bubbling.
They ate the pizza out on the back porch.
The air was cool, and the sky was turning pink.
Priya said it was the best pizza they had ever made.

passages.title: Sam's Map Game
sentences: On Monday after school, Sam drew a map of the playground near his house.
He drew the slide, the swings and a tall pine tree.
Then he hid a toy car under the bench by the swings.
He drew an X on that spot on the map.
Leo came to the playground at four o'clock.
Sam gave him the map.
Leo turned the map around and walked past the slide.
Five minutes later, Leo found the car.
"Now I will make a map for you," said Leo.

passages.title: The Geode
sentences: Mr. Varga opened a big box on the long table.
Inside were twenty round, gray rocks, each about the size of a tennis ball.
"These are geodes," he told the rock club.
"They look plain on the outside, but many are hollow, with crystals inside."
Maya picked the roughest rock in the box.
Everyone in the club put on safety glasses.
Mr. Varga showed Maya how to wrap her geode in a towel and tap it with a small hammer.
After three taps, the geode cracked into two pieces.
Inside, hundreds of tiny purple crystals shone in the light.
Mr. Varga said that the purple crystals were a mineral called amethyst.
The rock club meets in the back room of the library, and this was its last meeting before winter break.
At six o'clock, Maya wrapped both halves in paper and carried them home.

passages.title: A Whale Past Gull Island
sentences: The boat left the harbor at one o'clock on Saturday, with forty people on board.
Sam and Grandma Rose stood at the front rail and held on to their hats.
A guide in a green jacket spoke into a microphone.
She asked everyone to watch the water for a puff of mist called a blow.
A whale breathes out through a hole on top of its head, and the warm, wet air makes a cloud.
For almost an hour, the sea was empty and gray.
Then, far out past Gull Island, Sam saw a tall puff of white mist.
A humpback whale rose up, and its long, dark back slid through the waves.
Its tail lifted high into the air before it dove down.
Everyone on the boat cheered.
When the boat came back to the dock, it was almost four o'clock.

passages.title: The Dinosaur Talk
sentences: On Tuesday afternoon, the main hall of the library was full of people.
Forty chairs faced a big screen, and every chair was taken.
Dr. Bell from the museum had come to give a talk.
It was about dinosaurs with feathers, and it lasted one hour.
She held up a copy of a fossil from a small dinosaur.
The dinosaur was about as big as a turkey.
The rock around its bones showed the shapes of long feathers on its arms and tail.
Dr. Bell said that many small, meat-eating dinosaurs had feathers.
Scientists now think that birds came from dinosaurs like these.
Leo sat in the second row with Ana and Ben.
When the talk ended at five o'clock, Ana raised her hand.
She asked if a chicken is a kind of dinosaur.
Dr. Bell said that birds, like chickens, are close relatives of those small dinosaurs.
On the walk home, Ana drew a feathered dinosaur on the back of her program.

passages.title: The Skate Contest
sentences: The skate park in Harbor Town held a contest on a sunny Saturday in July.
Twelve skaters signed up, and each one had one minute to show their best tricks.
Leo was the ninth skater on the list.
While he waited, he sat on the fence beside the big ramp and watched the others.
Sam and Pixel stood near the gate with a sign that said GO LEO.
At eleven o'clock, after eight skaters had finished, the judge called Leo's name.
The judge was a woman in a blue helmet who once skated in big contests.
Leo rolled down the big ramp, turned around at the top of the other side and rolled back down.
His last trick was a jump over a low orange cone.
When the scores were read, Leo was in third place, and he got a small bronze medal.
After the contest, Leo, Sam and Pixel walked to Rose's Bakery for a snack.

passages.title: Ben at the Fair
sentences: On the second Saturday in August, the Harbor Town Summer Fair filled the school field with tents, games and food stands.
Near the gate, a small wooden stage stood under a striped roof.
At three o'clock, Ben carried his keyboard up the steps and plugged it in.
He had practiced four songs all month.
Ana sat in the front row with their mom and dad.
Ben played a fast song first, and some little children danced on the grass.
Then he played a slow song that he had written himself.
When he finished, a woman with a fair badge asked him to play one more song.
She was the person in charge of the whole fair.
Ben played a song from the twins' favorite video game, and the crowd cheered.

passages.title: Five Leaves for Friday
sentences: In October, the trees in Story Woods began to change color.
Ms. Ortiz told her class that leaves are green because of a substance called chlorophyll.
In autumn, many trees stop making it, and the yellow and orange colors in the leaves start to show.
She asked each student to bring five different leaves to class on Friday.
On Wednesday after school, Maya and Sam walked up the trail behind the campsite.
Pixel ran ahead and rolled in a pile of dry brown leaves.
Maya found a red maple leaf and a yellow birch leaf near the creek.
Sam found a brown oak leaf under a tall tree by the old mill.
By the time the sun set, they each had five leaves in a paper bag.
The next day, they pressed the leaves flat inside heavy books at Maya's house.

passages.title: The Maker Room
sentences: The new maker room opened in the basement of the Harbor Town library in March.
It has 3D printers, sewing machines and a long table full of robot parts.
On the first Saturday after it opened, Priya was waiting at the door at ten o'clock.
A young man with a name tag that said HELPER showed her around.
Priya wanted to build a robot arm that could pick up a pencil.
She used a small motor for the shoulder and another one for the elbow.
For the hand, she printed two plastic fingers that could open and close.
The first time she tested the arm, it dropped the pencil on the floor.
Priya added rubber bands to the fingers so they could grip better.
On the second try, the arm lifted the pencil and put it in a cup.
The helper wrote her name on the maker room's board for Builder of the Week.

passages.title: The Planet Walk
sentences: A row of nine metal signs stands along the path beside the harbor.
Together, they make a model of the solar system called the Planet Walk.
The first sign shows the Sun, and it stands outside the library.
The other eight signs show the planets in order.
On Sunday afternoon, Sam and Leo walked the whole path with Pixel.
Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars were all close to the Sun sign.
After Mars, the boys walked a long way before they reached Jupiter, near the ferry dock.
Saturn stood beside a row of fishing boats, and Uranus was next to a playground.
Neptune, the last planet, stood at the far end of the path, beside the seawall.
The walk from the Sun to Neptune took them 25 minutes.
Leo joked that Pixel was the first dog to walk past all the planets.

passages.title: The Bike Bus
sentences: Every Wednesday morning, a long line of bikes rolls through Harbor Town to the middle school.
People call it the Bike Bus, even though it has no engine.
It starts at Okafor's Bike Shop at eight o'clock, and riders join it at stops along the way.
Mr. Okafor rides at the front in a bright orange vest.
This week, Sam was waiting at the corner by Rose's Bakery with his helmet already on.
Grandma Rose waved from the shop window as he joined the line.
At the next stop, outside the library, Priya and Maya joined too.
The riders stopped at every red light and rode in a single line.
By the time the Bike Bus reached the school gate, it had twenty-two riders.
The first bell rang fifteen minutes later, at 8:30.

words.means: the motor that makes a car or bus move
a top with no sleeves, worn over clothes

passages.title: Calling the Space Station
sentences: On a Tuesday morning in November, the gym at Harbor Middle School was very quiet.
Two hundred students sat on the floor, facing a large screen and a table covered with radios and wires.
In a few minutes, the International Space Station would pass over the island, and the school had been chosen to talk to an astronaut on board.
The space station circles Earth about once every ninety minutes, about 400 kilometers above the ground.
Because it moves so fast, a radio on the ground can reach it for only about ten minutes at a time.
For weeks, a retired sailor with a white beard had been setting up an antenna on the gym roof.
His name is Mr. Dunn, and he leads the island's radio club.
At 10:42, a calm voice came through the speakers and said hello from space.
Ten students had written questions, and Priya was fourth in line.
Priya asked what the astronaut missed most about Earth.
The astronaut answered that she missed the sound of rain.
Nine minutes after the first hello, the voice faded into crackling noise as the station moved out of range.

passages.title: The Orienteering Race
sentences: Orienteering is a race in which runners use a map and a compass to find a series of checkpoints.
Each checkpoint is marked by an orange-and-white flag, and runners must reach the flags in the right order.
The fastest runner does not always win, because one wrong turn can add many minutes to a runner's time.
On the second Saturday in October, the Story Woods orienteering race began at the campsite.
Sam had studied the trail map for days, and he was the first person to sign up.
At nine o'clock, the organizer, a woman in a red cap, handed him a map with five circles drawn on it.
Sam was surprised to see that she was Ms. Ortiz, his science teacher, who had planned the course over the summer.
The first flag hung beside the old mill, and the second was on a bridge over the creek.
Sam reached the third flag, at the bottom of a rocky hill, after twenty minutes.
There, he checked his compass and saw that the fourth flag was due north, at the top of the hill.
Instead of following the long trail around the hill, he climbed straight up the gentle slope.
The fifth and last flag stood at the finish line, beside the lookout in Lantern Peaks.
Sam crossed the line fifty-two minutes after he started, and he finished in second place.

words.means: a tool with a needle that points north
places on the course that runners must reach
the side of a hill that goes up

passages.title: Gold in the Creek
sentences: More than a hundred years ago, a fisherman found a shiny yellow flake in the creek that runs through Story Woods.
It was gold, and within a year, hundreds of people had come to the island to search for more.
Most of them used a method called panning.
A miner scooped sand and water from the creek into a wide, shallow pan and swirled it around.
Gold is much heavier than sand, so the gold sank to the bottom of the pan while the light sand washed over the edge.
The gold rush on the island did not last long.
After about ten years, the creek had very little gold left, and most of the miners sailed home.
Today, the Ridgeway Mine Museum holds a gold panning day each summer, on the last Sunday in July.
Visitors stand in the shallow creek below the old mill and try panning for themselves.
Last year, Maya and Leo spent the whole morning there, with Mr. Varga showing them what to do.
Leo found only sand, but Maya found three tiny flakes, which she keeps in a glass jar on her desk.

passages.title: The Night of the Frogs
sentences: For most of the year, the wood frogs of Story Woods live quietly under fallen leaves on the forest floor.
Each spring, on the first warm, rainy night, they wake up and travel to the pond where they hatched, so they can lay their eggs.
To get there, many of them must cross Pond Lane, a narrow road between the woods and the water.
On that one night, the town closes the road to cars, and volunteers help the frogs across.
This year, the warm rain finally came on the second Friday in March.
As soon as it was dark, a small group gathered at the edge of Pond Lane with flashlights and buckets.
The group's leader, a tall man in a yellow raincoat, explained three rules.
Everyone had to walk slowly, carry each frog gently and always take it in the direction it was already going.
Sam, Maya and Priya worked together on one side of the road.
Sam held the flashlight, Priya carried the bucket and Maya kept count.
By ten o'clock, they had carried 112 frogs across, and the rain had almost stopped.
The next morning, Maya went back to the pond and heard the frogs calling, a sound like ducks quacking far away.

passages.title: The Pie Contest
sentences: The pie contest at the Harbor Town Fall Festival was on Saturday, and Grandma Rose had entered it for the first time.
On Friday night, she and Sam peeled and sliced twelve apples at the long steel table in the bakery's back kitchen.
Sam mixed the apples with sugar and cinnamon while Grandma Rose rolled out the crust.
They laid strips of dough across the top in a crisscross pattern.
Then they baked the pie in the big oven until the crust was golden.
Early the next morning, they carried the pie three blocks to the festival tent in the town square.
Twenty pies sat in a row on a long table, each with a card that showed a number but no name.
That way, the judges would not know who had baked each pie.
Three judges walked along the table, tasting a small piece of every pie and writing notes.
The first judge, a woman in a white apron, owns the Lighthouse Café, and her name is Mrs. Lin.
At noon, Mrs. Lin stood up and read the results.
Pie number 14, the apple pie with the crisscross top, had won second place.
That evening, back at the bakery, Grandma Rose hung the red ribbon above the cash register.

passages.title: The Library Tournament
sentences: The library's video game tournament lasted a whole weekend, and forty players signed up.
Every match was a race in the same racing game, played on two big screens in the community room.
The early rounds were on Saturday, and the last four players would meet in the final on Sunday afternoon.
Ana and Ben both won their first three races on Saturday.
In the fourth race, the twins had to play against each other.
Ben chose a heavy green truck, and Ana chose a small silver car that turned quickly.
Ana won by less than a second, and Ben shook her hand and said that he hoped she would win the final.
The final started at two o'clock the next day.
Ana raced against a high school student, a boy from Gull Island and a man who works at the bus station.
The race had five laps around a twisting mountain track.
Ana was in third place until the last lap, when she took a shortcut through a tunnel.
She crossed the line first, and the whole room cheered, especially Ben.

passages.title: The Long-Necked Visitor
sentences: Last winter, the Harbor Town museum got the biggest delivery it has ever had.
It was a copy of a Diplodocus skeleton, packed in thirty-eight wooden crates.
Diplodocus was a plant-eating dinosaur with a very long neck and an even longer tail.
The real animal was about twenty-six meters long, about as long as two school buses parked end to end.
The crates arrived at the harbor on a cargo boat on the second Monday in January.
A team of six builders from the mainland was waiting at the dock.
Their leader, a woman in a hard hat and a bright yellow jacket, checked each crate against a long list.
Her name is Ms. Lund, and she has built more than forty dinosaur skeletons.
The bones in the crates are not real fossils.
They are copies made of a light, strong plastic.
Each one was shaped in a mold taken from the bone of a real Diplodocus.
The builders spent three weeks putting the skeleton together on a steel frame.
They started with the legs and finished with the tip of the tail.
On the first Saturday in February, the museum opened the new hall to visitors.
Leo and Ben were near the front of the line, and Ben stood under the neck and looked straight up for a long time.

passages.title: Feeding Time
sentences: The Harbor Town Aquarium has only one octopus, and she is the most popular animal in the building.
An octopus can change the color of its skin in less than a second.
It can also squeeze its soft body through any gap bigger than its beak, which is the only hard part of its body.
Because of this, her tank has a heavy lid with no holes at all.
Every Saturday at two o'clock, a keeper feeds the octopus while visitors watch.
Last Saturday, Maya and Leo arrived at half past one.
First they went to the touch tank by the entrance.
There, they gently touched a sea star and a sea cucumber with two fingers, as the sign asked.
Twenty minutes later, they hurried upstairs to find seats in front of the octopus tank.
At two o'clock, a young woman in a blue shirt climbed a short ladder beside the tank.
She was the aquarium's animal keeper, and she has cared for the octopus for three years.
She dropped a closed plastic jar with a crab inside into the water.
The octopus turned from brown to dark red.
It wrapped two arms around the jar and twisted off the lid in less than a minute.
Everyone clapped, and Maya drew the octopus in her sketchbook before they left at three o'clock.

passages.title: The Recording
sentences: The island's radio station plays music by local musicians every Sunday evening.
This year, the station asked Ms. Gray to choose three students to record a song in its studio.
She chose Priya, a cellist, and two older students who are violinists.
The recording was set for the Tuesday before winter break, at four o'clock.
That afternoon, Ms. Gray drove the three students to a small brick building behind the bus station.
Inside, a man wearing large headphones sat behind a desk covered in buttons and sliders.
He was the sound engineer, the person who records the music and makes it sound clear, and his name was Mr. Quinn.
He placed a microphone in front of each instrument and asked the students to play a few notes.
The first try was too fast, and the second try had a wrong note.
On the third try, the three students played the whole song without a mistake.
Mr. Quinn played it back through the speakers, and Priya could hear every note of her cello.
Twelve days later, the song was played on the radio, and Priya's whole family listened in the kitchen.

passages.title: The Greenhouse Robot
sentences: Behind Harbor Middle School there is a glass greenhouse where the science classes grow tomatoes, beans and herbs.
The plants need water every day, even on weekends, when the school is empty.
For years, Ms. Ortiz drove to school every Saturday and Sunday to water them by hand.
In January, the robotics club decided to solve the problem.
Priya and two other members built a small robot that rolls along a track between the rows of plants.
A sensor pushed into the soil measures how wet it is, and the robot waters only the plants that are dry.
They tested it in the robotics room for three weeks before they moved it to the greenhouse.
The first real test came on the weekend of the big February snowstorm, when nobody could reach the school.
On Monday morning, after the snowplows had cleared the roads, Priya hurried to the greenhouse before the first bell.
The tomato plants were green and healthy, and the robot was parked at the end of its track.
Ms. Ortiz said it was the first weekend in four years that she had stayed home.

words.means: a glass building where plants are grown
a part that checks how wet the soil is
trucks with a big blade that clear the roads in winter

passages.title: Lightning Delay
sentences: Lightning can hit the ground far away from the storm cloud that makes it.
So sports teams follow a simple rule.
When anyone hears thunder, everyone must leave the field and go inside a building or a car.
Play can start again only after thirty minutes have passed without any thunder.
On the first Saturday in June, Ana and Ben's team was playing a home game at Pier Field.
The sky was bright when the game started at ten o'clock, but dark clouds were gathering over Lantern Peaks.
Twenty minutes into the game, the players heard a low rumble of thunder.
The referee, a young woman with a whistle on a red cord, blew three short blasts and pointed at the clubhouse.
Both teams walked quickly off the field and waited inside while heavy rain fell on the roof.
Ben watched the clubhouse clock, and Ana counted the seconds between each flash and its thunder.
The last thunder came at 10:45, and the storm moved out over the sea.
Thirty minutes later, the referee blew her whistle again, and the teams ran back onto the wet grass.
The twins' team won the game two to one, and Ana scored the winning goal.

passages.title: The Eclipse
sentences: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon passes between the Sun and Earth and blocks some or all of the Sun's light.
During a partial eclipse, the Moon covers only part of the Sun, so the bright disk slowly turns into a curved crescent.
It is never safe to look straight at the Sun, even during an eclipse, so people use special eclipse glasses or project the Sun's image onto paper.
The island's most recent eclipse happened on a school day in early April.
Weeks before, Ms. Ortiz had ordered a pair of eclipse glasses for every student.
She had also invited a guest: a scientist who studies distant galaxies at the observatory on Lantern Peaks.
The guest was Dr. Hale, and she arrived with a telescope fitted with a dark filter that made the Sun safe to view.
Just after lunch, the whole school gathered on the soccer field behind the gym, and at 1:10 the Moon began to slide across the edge of the Sun.
Leo had brought a kitchen colander from home.
When he held it above a sheet of white paper, dozens of tiny crescents appeared in its shadow, one for every hole.
Priya made a pinhole viewer from a cereal box, and Sam wrote down the time of each change in a notebook.
At the middle of the eclipse, the Moon covered most of the Sun, and the air felt noticeably cooler.
The eclipse lasted two and a half hours from start to finish.
By the time the Moon moved completely away from the Sun, the school buses were already lined up in front of the school.

passages.title: A Hundred Years of the Coast Railway
sentences: This spring, the coast railway celebrated its hundredth birthday.
Before the line opened, the only ways to travel from Harbor Town to the villages along the north shore were by boat or on horseback.
Building the railway took four years, because workers had to cut a path through rocky hills and build eleven bridges over streams and inlets.
The first trains were pulled by steam engines.
A worker called a fireman shoveled coal into a firebox, and the heat boiled water in a large tank called a boiler.
The steam pushed on pistons, which turned the wheels.
In those days, a trip from Harbor Town to Shell Beach took almost two hours, because the train stopped at every village.
Today the same trip takes one hour, and the trains run on diesel engines.
To celebrate the birthday, the railway brought an old steam engine back to the island for one weekend in May.
On Saturday morning, a crowd gathered at the train station in Harbor Town, where the engine stood hissing beside the platform.
The driver, an older man in a striped cap and blue overalls, leaned out of the cab to wave.
He had driven trains on the coast line for thirty years before he retired, and he had learned to drive a steam engine just for this weekend.
Sam and Grandma Rose rode the steam train to Shell Beach and back.
The trip took longer than usual, because people stood on every bridge to wave as it passed.

passages.title: Mapping the Bottom of the Bay
sentences: Most maps show roads, rivers and towns, but some of the most useful maps show a place that no one can see: the bottom of the sea.
These maps are called charts, and ship captains use them to stay away from rocks and shallow water.
To make a chart, a survey boat travels slowly back and forth across the water in long, straight lines.
A device under the boat sends a pulse of sound down to the seabed and listens for the echo.
The longer the echo takes to return, the deeper the water is.
Last summer, a survey boat from the mainland spent three weeks mapping the bay around Harbor Town.
The harbor had not been charted for forty years, and storms had moved large amounts of sand since then.
The boat's chief scientist, a woman with short gray hair, gave a talk at the library on her last evening on the island.
Her name is Dr. Shaw, and she has mapped the seafloor in every ocean on Earth.
Sam sat in the front row with his notebook.
Dr. Shaw showed a colorful chart on the screen, with deep water in dark blue and shallow water in yellow.
Sam noticed a long yellow strip near the harbor entrance that was not on the old chart.
Dr. Shaw explained that it was a new sandbar, a long hill of sand under the water, and that the ferry's route would move slightly north to avoid it.
Two weeks after the talk, Captain Ruth Lane steered the ferry along the new route for the first time.
Sam watched from the seawall, holding the copy of the chart that Dr. Shaw had given him.

passages.title: Rocks in the Dark
sentences: Some minerals look plain in daylight but glow in bright colors under ultraviolet light.
Ultraviolet light, often called UV light, is a kind of light that human eyes cannot see.
When it shines on certain minerals, they give off light that we can see, and the colors can be surprising: fluorite often glows blue, and calcite can glow red.
Every year on the last Friday in October, the Ridgeway Mine Museum in Lantern Peaks holds an evening tour called Rocks in the Dark.
This year, the rock club met at the museum's front door at seven o'clock, just after sunset.
Their guide for the night was a short man with a lamp on his hard hat, and he led them down a long wooden staircase into the oldest tunnel.
It was Mr. Varga, who leads the rock club and also gives tours at the museum.
At the bottom, Mr. Varga asked everyone to switch off their lamps.
For a moment, the tunnel was completely black.
Then he turned on a small UV lamp and pointed it at the wall.
Streaks of green and red glowed in the rock, and Maya gasped so loudly that the sound echoed down the tunnel.
Mr. Varga explained that the green came from a mineral called willemite, and the red came from calcite.
Forty-five minutes after the tour began, the club climbed back up the staircase.
In the gift shop, Maya spent her saved money on a small piece of fluorite and a tiny UV flashlight, and Mr. Varga reminded her never to shine it into anyone's eyes.
That night, in her bedroom, she switched off the lights and watched the fluorite glow blue.

passages.title: The Museum Sleepover
sentences: Twice a year, the Harbor Town museum invites a small group of students to sleep overnight in its dinosaur hall.
The spring sleepover was on the third Friday in April, and Ana, Ben and Leo were among the twenty students chosen.
They arrived at half past six in the evening, carrying sleeping bags, pillows and flashlights.
The evening began with a tour led by the museum's fossil expert, a woman with reading glasses on a chain around her neck.
She introduced herself as Dr. Bell and said that she had been digging up fossils for twenty-five years.
She showed them the new Tyrannosaurus skull, which had arrived from a museum on the mainland only a week before.
The skull was about as long as Ben is tall.
After a snack of popcorn in the museum café, the students spread their sleeping bags on the floor beneath the Triceratops skeleton.
At nine o'clock, Dr. Bell turned off the main lights, and the students explored the hall with their flashlights.
Leo pointed his flashlight at the Triceratops skull and made the shadow of its horns stretch across the ceiling.
Lights out was at half past ten, but most of the students whispered for another hour.
The next morning, a guard woke everyone at seven o'clock.
They ate breakfast in the café, rolled up their sleeping bags and were picked up by their families two hours later, just before the museum opened its doors to visitors.

words.means: all the bones of a body, put together
old bones or shapes kept in rock

passages.title: A Robot That Cleans the Harbor
sentences: Every day, wind and rain carry plastic bottles, bags and wrappers into the harbor.
Much of this trash floats near the docks, where the wind pushes it into corners.
Last fall, the town tried a new way to clean it up: a small robot boat that works on its own.
The robot is about the size of a bathtub, with two floating hulls and a wide net between them.
Solar panels on its roof charge its battery, so it never needs fuel.
Cameras and sensors help it steer around boats, docks and birds.
When its net is full, it returns to its station at the end of the fishing pier to be emptied.
The person who looks after the robot is a young engineer who grew up in Harbor Town.
Her name is Ms. Kaur, and she first saw a robot like this one while she was studying at a university on the mainland.
In its first month, the robot collected more than two thousand plastic bottles.
In March, Ms. Kaur visited the robotics club at Harbor Middle School.
She showed the students a video of the robot at work, and Priya asked how it knows when its net is full.
Ms. Kaur explained that a sensor weighs the net, and when the net is heavy enough, the robot heads back to its station.
Two days later, the club wrote a letter to the town council to ask if students could help test the next robot.

passages.title: The Sugar Shack
sentences: Maple syrup begins as sap, a thin, clear liquid that flows inside maple trees.
The sap runs best in early spring, when the nights are below freezing and the days are warm.
Farmers drill a small hole in each tree and collect the sap in buckets or through long plastic tubes.
Then they boil it for hours, until most of the water has turned to steam and only thick, sweet syrup is left.
It takes about forty liters of sap to make one liter of syrup.
Every March, a family farm on the far side of Story Woods opens its sugar shack to visitors for two weekends.
A sugar shack is a small wooden building where the sap is boiled.
This year, Ana, Ben and their mom drove out on the second Saturday of the month, the morning after a hard frost.
A tall man in a red wool jacket met them at the gate with a wagon pulled by two horses.
He was Mr. Dale, the farmer, and his family has made syrup on the same land for more than a hundred years.
The wagon carried them into the woods, where thin blue tubes ran from tree to tree and down the hill to a large tank.
Mr. Dale let Ben taste a drop of sap, which was only a little sweet, almost like water.
Then they rode to the sugar shack, where clouds of steam rose from the roof.
Inside, the sap bubbled in a long metal pan over a wood fire.
At noon, everyone ate pancakes with fresh syrup at long tables outside the shack.
Before they left, Ana bought a small bottle of syrup to take home, and Ben said it was the sweetest thing he had ever tasted.

passages.title: Midsummer Music Day
sentences: On the longest day of the year, Harbor Town holds Midsummer Music Day, a free concert that lasts from noon until sunset.
Bands play on three stages: one on the ferry dock, one in the town square and one on the grass beside the lighthouse.
This year, Ms. Gray's Grade 7 band was invited to play on the town square stage at two o'clock.
The band arrived an hour early to set up.
Leo tightened the screws on his drums while the rest of the band tuned their instruments.
Ben spent the afternoon helping a man in a straw hat carry speakers to the ferry dock stage.
The man in the straw hat was the festival's sound director, and he was Mr. Quinn, the same engineer who records music at the island's radio station.
The band's set lasted forty minutes.
Leo kept a steady beat through all six songs, and Ana and Maya clapped along from the front row.
When the set was over, Leo, Ana and Maya walked across town to the lighthouse stage to hear a fiddle group from Gull Island.
Sunset came at almost nine o'clock that night.
As the last song ended, Ben finally joined his friends on the grass beside the lighthouse, tired but smiling.

passages.title: The King Tide
sentences: A few times each year, the tides along the coast rise much higher than usual.
People call these extra-high tides king tides.
They happen when the Moon is at its closest to Earth and lines up with the Sun, so the pull of both is added together.
Scientists can work out the day and time of each king tide years in advance.
In early January, Ms. Ortiz learned that the year's highest king tide would arrive on the third Saturday in January, at 11:20 in the morning.
She asked her science club to measure it.
Priya built a tide gauge, a tall pole with a line painted every ten centimeters, and tied it to the ladder at the end of the ferry dock.
At nine o'clock on that Saturday, the water was just below the third line.
Sam and Maya stood on the seawall with clipboards, and every fifteen minutes Priya called out a new number.
There was almost no wind that day, so the water rose slowly and smoothly.
When the water finally stopped rising, it had reached the ninth line, the highest mark the club had ever seen.
By lunchtime, the water was going down again, and the fishing boats beside the dock were slowly getting lower as the tide went out.
That afternoon, the club pinned a photo of the gauge on the science room wall, next to the date and the time of the highest water.

passages.title: The Salmon Run
sentences: Salmon begin their lives in fresh water, in streams and creeks far from the sea.
After a year or two, the young fish swim downstream to the ocean, where they grow large and strong.
Years later, each adult salmon swims back to the same stream where it hatched, using its sense of smell to find the way.
There, the salmon lay their eggs in the gravel, and the cycle begins again.
In Story Woods, the salmon return to the creek every autumn, usually in the first two weeks of October.
This year, the first fish were seen on the morning of Tuesday, October 3, below the old mill.
A park ranger who has counted the salmon for many years put a notice on the trail board.
It asked visitors to stay on the bank and keep dogs on leashes, so the fish could rest in the shallow pools.
The following Saturday, Sam and Grandma Rose packed a lunch and walked to the creek with Pixel on his leash.
They stood on the wooden bridge, where the water was clear and slow.
Below them, dozens of red salmon waited in a deep pool, their tails moving gently in the current.
Sam counted forty-one fish before Pixel lay down on the bridge for a nap.
On the way home, they met the ranger, a woman in a green uniform carrying a clipboard.
She told them that this year's count had already passed two thousand fish.

passages.title: The Island Loop
sentences: Every summer, cyclists from all over the region come to Harbor Town for the Island Loop, a bike race that follows the coast road all the way around the island.
The loop is eighty kilometers long, and the fastest riders finish in a little over two hours.
There is also a shorter family ride of twenty kilometers, which ends at the lookout on Lantern Peaks.
This year, the race was held on the second Sunday in August.
Leo and his dad entered the family ride, and they were at the starting line in front of Okafor's Bike Shop by half past seven.
Before the start, a man with a toolbox checked every bike's brakes and tires.
It was Mr. Okafor, who has checked bikes for the race every year since it began.
The big race started at eight o'clock, and the family ride left thirty minutes later.
The family ride followed the coast road past the harbor and the fishing piers, and then it turned inland toward the hills.
The last five kilometers were a steep climb, and Leo had to stand up on his pedals to keep going.
He and his dad reached the lookout an hour and a half after they started.
They ate sandwiches at the top and watched the fast riders far below, racing along the coast road in a long, colorful line.
Leo said his legs felt very tired, and his dad laughed and said that his legs did too.

passages.title: The Bus to Art Class
sentences: On Tuesday morning, Maya waited at the bus station in Harbor Town.
She had her sketchbook and a bag of pencils.
Her art class was at the library at nine o'clock.
Bus 2 came at a quarter past eight.
Maya sat by the window and drew the boats in the harbor.
Ben got on at the next stop.
He sat down next to her and looked at her drawing.
"That boat looks real," he said.
They got off the bus together at the library.
Ben was going to the art class too.

passages.title: Counting Seals
sentences: On Sunday morning, Priya and her dad took the ferry to Gull Island.
They walked to the flat rocks on the north beach.
Twelve seals were asleep in the warm sun.
Priya stayed behind the rope and counted them with her binoculars.
At eleven o'clock, Ranger Jo came along the path.
She wrote Priya's number in her notebook.
"Twelve is the most this week," said Ranger Jo.
After lunch, Priya and her dad took the ferry home.

passages.title: The Fish Kite
sentences: On Saturday afternoon, Leo and Sam went to Windy Cape.
The wind was strong, and the grass on the cliff top was bent flat.
Leo had a green kite shaped like a fish.
Sam held the kite up, and Leo let out the string.
The fish kite rose quickly into the sky.
A woman in a blue pilot's jacket watched them from a bench.
Her name was Captain Ada.
"Keep the string tight," she said, "and stay far from the cliff edge."
At five o'clock, the boys rolled up the string and packed the kite away.

passages.title: Monday at Cloud Hill
sentences: On Monday morning, Captain Ada drove up the road to Cloud Hill.
Thick fog sat on the hill, so no planes could fly yet.
Captain Ada parked by the old hangar and went in.
Inside the hangar, Mr. Lund was at work on the Kookaburra.
Mr. Lund fixes planes at Cloud Hill.
He was taking the old tires off the small red plane.
Then Rosa came to the door and waved.
Rosa drives the fuel truck.
She would come back on Friday to fill the plane with fuel.
By ten o'clock, the fog was gone, and the sun shone on the plane.

passages.title: Take-off Morning
sentences: On Monday morning, the Kookaburra rolled out of the old hangar.
Mr. Lund and Nell pushed it onto the grass by the runway.
Then Captain Ada climbed into the cockpit.
The cockpit is the front part of the plane, where the pilot sits.
She put on her seat belt.
She checked the fuel, the radio and the map one last time.
Then the engine started, and the propeller began to spin.
Nell waved to her from behind the fence.
The plane rolled down the long runway and went up into the sky.

passages.title: Breakfast for the Koalas
sentences: Every morning at seven, Ranger Tess gets in her truck.
She drives to the edge of the woods.
There, she cuts fresh branches from tall gum trees.
Then she drives back to the sanctuary.
She puts the branches up high in the koala yards.
A koala named Gumnut sniffs the leaves.
Then Gumnut starts to eat.
Koalas only eat the kinds of leaves they like.
By eight, every koala has a fresh breakfast.

passages.title: The Balloon at Six
sentences: On Saturday, Ana woke up early at Star Point.
It was still dark outside her window.
At a quarter to six, she walked down the lamp path to the weather station.
Dr. Amal was there with a big white balloon.
A small box hung on a string under it.
"This box measures the air," said Dr. Amal.
"It sends the numbers back by radio."
At six o'clock, Dr. Amal let go of the string.
The balloon rose fast over the white dome.
Soon it was only a tiny dot in the sky.
Then Ana went back up the path to eat breakfast.

passages.title: Leo and Max on the Coast Line
sentences: On Saturday afternoon, Leo took his cousin Max to Pier Station.
Max is seven, and he had never been on a train.
Their train came in at two o'clock.
Max sat by the window and pointed at the waves.
The train stopped at Shell Halt, but they stayed in their seats.
At half past two, the train reached Rail Coast.
Leo and Max got off and walked to the station clock.
Mr. Haddad waved to them from the signal box.
Max waved back with both hands.

passages.title: Maya's Coiled Stone
sentences: On Thursday morning, Maya and Grandma Rose took the boat to Fossil Bay.
They landed at the pier and walked down to the beach.
Tall gray cliffs stood above the beach.
Maya looked at the loose stones near the water.
Beside a big flat rock, she found a round gray stone.
A coiled shell was pressed into one side of it.
Maya carried the stone to Dr. Bell's tent at the far end of the beach.
"This is an ammonite," said Dr. Bell.
"It was a sea animal that lived long ago, in the time of the dinosaurs."

passages.title: Turtle Tracks After Dark
sentences: On Friday night, Ana and Ben walked along the beach on Reef Island with Mari.
Mari carried a small red flashlight.
She said that bright white light can confuse sea turtles.
Near the top of the beach, Ben stopped and pointed at the sand.
A wide trail of marks went from the water up to the dry sand.
Another trail went back down to the sea.
"Those are turtle tracks," said Mari.
"A mother turtle came up here to lay her eggs."
Ana wrote the date in her notebook, and they walked back very quietly.

items.explain: They visited on October 7. The first fish were seen on Tuesday, October 3, and the third paragraph says they went the following Saturday. Four days after Tuesday, October 3, is Saturday, October 7.

items.prompt: Who is the woman in the green uniform?
options: The park ranger who counts the salmon
items.hint: The last paragraph says "the ranger". Look back to the second paragraph to find what the ranger does.
items.explain: She is the park ranger who counts the salmon. The second paragraph says the ranger counts the salmon and put up the notice, and the last paragraph says the ranger wore a green uniform.

items.prompt: Tap the sentence that tells when the salmon usually come back to the creek in Story Woods.
items.hint: Look for the word "usually". This year's date is a different sentence.
items.explain: The salmon usually come back in the first two weeks of October. It is the first sentence of the second paragraph.

items.prompt: What time did Leo and his dad reach the lookout?
items.hint: Find the time the family ride started. It is not eight o'clock. Then find how long the ride took, and count forward.
items.explain: They reached the lookout at 10:00. The family ride left thirty minutes after eight, at 8:30, and the third paragraph says they arrived an hour and a half later.

items.prompt: Who is the man with the toolbox?
options: Mr. Okafor, who owns the bike shop
A race judge from the lookout
items.hint: Find the toolbox. Read the next sentence to find out who he is.
items.explain: He is Mr. Okafor. The second paragraph says a man with a toolbox checked the bikes, and the next sentence gives his name.

items.prompt: Build a sentence about where and when Leo rode.
items.frame: Leo and his dad started at {0} and finished at {1} on {2}.
items.hint: The finish of the family ride is in the first paragraph. The day and the starting line are in the second paragraph.
items.explain: Leo and his dad started at Okafor's Bike Shop and finished at the lookout on Lantern Peaks on the second Sunday in August. The first paragraph says where the family ride ends, and the second paragraph gives the day and the start.

items.prompt: Where was Maya's art class?
items.hint: Find the sentence with the words art class. Look for a place in it.
items.explain: Maya's art class was at the library. It is in the third sentence.

items.prompt: When did Priya and her dad take the ferry home?
items.hint: Find the sentence about going home. Look for a time word in it.
items.explain: They took the ferry home after lunch. It is in the last sentence.

items.prompt: Who told the boys to stay far from the cliff edge?
items.hint: Find the words cliff edge. Then look back to see who "she" is.
items.explain: Captain Ada told them. The sentence before it says her name.

items.prompt: Who was at work on the Kookaburra when Captain Ada went into the hangar?
items.hint: Find the sentence where Captain Ada goes in. Then read the next sentence to see who was inside the hangar.
items.explain: Mr. Lund was at work on the Kookaburra. The fourth sentence says he was inside the hangar, working on it.

items.prompt: When did the Kookaburra roll out of the hangar?
items.hint: Look for the words that tell the day and the time of day.
items.explain: It rolled out on Monday morning. The first sentence tells the day and the time of day.

items.prompt: Where does Ranger Tess cut the fresh branches?
options: At the edge of the woods
items.hint: Find the sentence about cutting branches. The word "There" points back to a place in the sentence before it.
items.explain: She cuts them at the edge of the woods. The second sentence names the place, and the word "There" in the third sentence points back to it.

items.prompt: When did Dr. Amal let go of the balloon?
items.hint: Find the sentence where Dr. Amal lets go. Look for a time word in it.
items.explain: Dr. Amal let go at six o'clock. It is in the sentence about letting go of the string. A quarter to six is when Ana walked down the path.

items.prompt: Where did Leo and Max get off the train?
items.hint: Find the sentence where they get off. Then read the sentence just before it to find the place.
items.explain: They got off at Rail Coast. The train reached Rail Coast, and then they got off. At Shell Halt, they stayed in their seats.

items.prompt: Where did Maya find the round gray stone?
items.hint: Find the sentence where Maya finds the stone. Look for a place word in it.
items.explain: She found it beside a big flat rock. It is in the sentence where she finds the stone. She carried it to the tent later.

items.prompt: Who saw the turtle tracks first?
items.hint: Find the sentence where someone stops and points at the sand.
items.explain: Ben saw the tracks first. He stopped and pointed at the sand before Mari said what the marks were.

steps.say: A story map has three boxes: who, where and when. I will look for each one in the story.
Who is the story about? I look for a name. The first sentence says Leo.
Where did Leo go? I look for a place. The first sentence says the skate park.
When did he go? I look for a day or a part of the day. It says Saturday morning.
So my story map is: Leo, the skate park, Saturday morning.
